claims.text: Applying a thin aluminum-resistant interlayer by CVD to boride-based components will reduce corrosion in molten aluminum.
Conventional uncoated boride-based components are vulnerable to direct attack by molten aluminum at approximately 660°C.
CVD can produce a thin, uniform protective layer suitable for the proposed application.
A nitride or oxide coating can remain stable at the high temperatures relevant to molten-aluminum exposure.
A continuous, well-adhered interlayer will act as a diffusion and chemical-reaction barrier between the boride substrate and molten aluminum.
The protective interlayer will limit direct contact between the boride surface and molten aluminum.
Limiting direct contact will reduce deleterious interfacial reactions and metal diffusion.
The barrier effect will stabilize the component surface and prevent corrosion pits.
The barrier effect will prevent formation of degrading intermetallic phases during molten-aluminum exposure.
Coated boride components will have lower corrosion current density than uncoated components under equivalent molten-aluminum exposure.
Coated boride components will have less weight loss than uncoated components under equivalent molten-aluminum exposure.
Coated boride components will exhibit fewer surface defects than uncoated components after molten-aluminum exposure.
The intervention will remain effective during continuous exposure at approximately 660°C as long as the coating remains uniform, well adhered, and intact.
Thermal stresses and nonoptimized coating thickness can reduce the coating's effectiveness.
Cyclic thermal and mechanical loading may cause long-term coating delamination.
